personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Ron is defined by a rich cluster of traits that operate simultaneously and sometimes in tension: loyal warmth toward Harry, sharp humor (often self-deprecating or directed at targets he finds absurd), genuine enthusiasm for Quidditch and Krum, fierce pride that is easily wounded by insecurity about money and status, impulsive moral courage (defending Hermione against Malfoy, standing up to Crouch), and a tendency to be petty and stubborn when jealous. His voice is distinctive: short declarative sentences, spontaneous outbursts, sarcasm that functions as a social weapon, blunt observations, and moments of surprising perceptiveness ('your mother won't be happy, Ron'). He is quick to mock but also quick to apologize when he knows he is wrong. His jealousy of Harry is not malice but wounded pride, and it coexists with genuine devotion. He is funny in ways that are not just comic relief — his humor often has social intelligence behind it (mocking Percy's cauldron report, imitating Trelawney, inventing doom-laden Divination predictions with Harry). He is also emotionally reactive in ways the books do not sanitize: he says genuinely unkind things about Padma's nose, about Eloise Midgen, about Hermione going with Krum.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves the broad outline: Ron is enthusiastic, loyal, funny, and jealous of Harry. His Krum obsession is fully present and played for comedy. His jealousy after Harry's name comes out of the Goblet is present and reasonably faithful in its beats. His bluntness is preserved in several exchanges. His humor lands — 'bloody hell' as a recurring verbal tic, the dress robes scene, asking Krum for his autograph at the end. The film also preserves his impulsive protectiveness: shouting at Barty Crouch after the wand-pointing incident, defending Harry at the second task scores, his 'even when you go wrong it turns out right' reaction.
personality_voice.difference: The film loses significant texture. Ron's extended interior sarcasm — the sustained mockery of Percy, his running commentary during Divination, the Trelawney imitation, the shared Divination homework invention with Harry — is mostly absent. His voice in the film is more reactive and less verbally inventive. The jealousy arc is present but compressed to a few confrontational lines rather than a sustained behavioural pattern. His pettiness toward Hermione at the Yule Ball ('he's using you'; 'I doubt it, he's way too old') is present but stripped of the full context of resentment that the books provide. Several speech patterns that define him in the books — his habit of blunt social commentary, his capacity for self-aware humour about his own failings — appear only sporadically. His apology scene after the first task is notably shortened and his explanation ('I was a bit distraught') is played more as comedy than genuine emotional reckoning. The film does not show his sustained period of cold-shouldering Harry across weeks of school, which is crucial to understanding the depth of his insecurity. Additionally, his voice in the film is often reduced to short reactive exclamations rather than the longer, more elaborate verbal constructions of the books.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core personality is recognizable and the main traits — loyalty, humor, jealousy, Quidditch enthusiasm — are present. The penalty applies because important secondary traits are lost or flattened: his sustained verbal wit, his capacity for unkind pettiness (socially revealing rather than played as pure comedy), his stubborn pride that extends beyond the Goblet incident, and the emotional complexity of his jealousy. The film preserves the skeleton but not the full texture of his voice. This places him in the 14–17 band.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the books, Ron serves several active narrative functions in Goblet of Fire: he is Harry's primary emotional sounding board whose absence during weeks of estrangement is narratively significant; he is an active participant in research and preparation for all three tasks (Summoning Charm practice, Impediment Curse sessions, the library search on the second task); he provides contextual wizarding knowledge Harry lacks (explaining the Dark Mark, giants, the Imperius Curse, Crouch's history); he asks Sirius probing questions in the cave scene; he proposes theories and analyses (Bagman paying in leprechaun gold, Karkaroff as a suspect, Percy and Crouch); he is the one who resolves the estrangement by coming to Harry after the first task. He causes changes in other characters and in the direction of scenes. In the second task, his role as the thing Harry will miss most gives him narrative weight.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film preserves Ron's role as Harry's companion and emotional anchor. His presence at the World Cup, his estrangement and reconciliation, his participation in the Yule Ball subplot, his second-task function, and his role in the final hospital scene are all present. He is present in most key scenes. Some of his expository function is preserved (explaining the Dark Mark to Harry at the campsite, his reaction to Krum's arrival).
narrative_role_agency.difference: Substantial agency losses occur throughout. The book's multi-week estrangement with documented scenes across the school year is compressed into one confrontation scene. Ron's active role in research for the second task — he, Harry and Hermione spend weeks in the library — is almost entirely absent from the film; the task preparation is barely shown. His role in the cave scene with Sirius, where he asks substantive questions and pushes Sirius on Crouch and Snape, is gone (the Sirius cave meeting does not appear in the film). His analysis of the Bagman/leprechaun gold situation, his theories about Karkaroff and the Death Eaters, and his contribution to the Crouch mystery are cut. He does not contribute to the intellectual work of the story in the film — he is primarily a reactive presence. Several key expository functions are transferred: Hermione explains the Dark Mark in detail at the campsite (in the books Ron also contributes), and Hermione's agency in preparation scenes exceeds Ron's to a greater degree than in the books. His claim at the end ('I told you, I was distraught') attempts to retroactively credit him with the Hagrid warning chain but this is played as comedy rather than genuine plot contribution. The Karkaroff's arm scene (cut per non-theatrical exclusion) further removes a beat that showed Ron's reactive engagement with the Death Eater theme.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Ron retains a recognizable narrative role as loyal friend and second-task hostage, but his agency as an active co-investigator, theorist, and participant in preparation is substantially reduced. Several intellectual and analytical contributions are cut. His expository function is partially retained but diminished. This is a clear case of role compression that removes defining narrative contributions. Score in the 10–13 range.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Ron's central motivation in Goblet of Fire is the tension between devoted friendship and the accumulating weight of being Harry's best friend — always in Harry's shadow, never recognized on his own terms, from a poor family that can't give him the material and social standing he craves. His estrangement from Harry is not petty jealousy: it is the product of years of insecurity (the dress robes, the secondhand everything, being the sixth child in a family of high achievers, watching Harry get money and fame and attention without asking for it). He also has a secondary motivation around status (wanting Krum's autograph, dreaming about entering the tournament himself, fantasizing about winning). The conflict between his love for Harry and his resentment is rendered in detail: he avoids Harry's eyes, sits with Dean and Seamus, says genuinely cutting things, but also cannot maintain the estrangement once he sees Harry actually in danger. His jealousy of Krum for Hermione is similarly motivated by a mix of protectiveness, wounded pride, and unacknowledged feeling.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film preserves the core motivation: jealousy born from being permanently in Harry's shadow. The confrontation scene ('Ron Weasley, Harry Potter's stupid friend') articulates this directly and more explicitly than any single speech in the books. His insecurity about money is briefly present (the dress robes). His jealousy of Krum for Hermione is shown at the Yule Ball. His reconciliation is emotionally present.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The film delivers the motivation more bluntly and less through accumulated evidence. In the books, the motivation is built across weeks of observable behaviour; in the film it is stated in one scene. This means the internal conflict is present but simplified — stated rather than dramatized. The leprechaun gold scene ('I hate being poor') which articulates his class insecurity is absent. The sustained weeks of petty behaviour that demonstrate the depth of the conflict are compressed. His jealousy of Krum for Hermione lacks the full context of his unresolved feelings that the books build. However, the core motivation is not changed or replaced — it is merely underexplained relative to the books.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are simplified but substantially correct. The film states what the books dramatize. The core conflict (shadow/jealousy/insecurity) is intact even if the texture and accumulation are lost. This is simplification, not substitution. Score in the 11–13 range.

character_arc.book_baseline: Ron's arc in Goblet of Fire follows a clear trajectory: starting point of loyal but insecure best friendship → rupture caused by jealousy and wounded pride → weeks of stubborn estrangement during which Harry is genuinely alone → turning point at the first task when danger makes the jealousy seem petty → reconciliation and renewed friendship with a degree of growth → further complications (Yule Ball argument with Hermione, Krum jealousy, the leprechaun gold admission) → final consolidation of friendship through shared trauma. The arc is not dramatic personal transformation but it has real steps: Ron recognizes he was wrong, apologizes (however briefly), and re-commits. Importantly, the arc includes his failure at the Yule Ball — he has not fully resolved his insecurity about Hermione — which means the arc is not falsely resolved.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film reproduces the basic shape: friendship → estrangement after Goblet announcement → reconciliation after first task → Yule Ball friction with Hermione → restored friendship in the hospital wing. The reconciliation scene ('I reckon you'd have to be barking mad to put your name in that cup') is present but restructured so Ron retroactively claims he was trying to warn Harry (the Hagrid message chain), which muddies the emotional clarity of his admission that he was wrong. The Yule Ball rupture with Hermione is present.
character_arc.difference: The multi-week arc is severely compressed. In the books, the estrangement occupies chapters and has documented daily texture (sitting with Dean and Seamus, not speaking in Charms, the Snape dungeon detention side-by-side, the Hogsmeade visit invisibility cloak scene). In the film, the estrangement is established in one dormitory scene and the reconciliation follows almost immediately at the first task. The arc's steps are present but the duration and weight of each step is drastically reduced. The leprechaun gold admission ('I hate being poor') which marks a moment of Ron acknowledging his own material insecurity directly is absent. The Yule Ball argument with Hermione is present but its aftermath — the awkward unresolved peace, the 'unspoken agreement not to discuss it' — is not shown. The film's version of Ron's reconciliation also partially undermines his growth by having him claim credit for a circuitous warning rather than straightforwardly acknowledging he was wrong, which softens the arc's emotional honesty.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc exists and has the correct shape, but important steps are rushed or missing. The compression changes the emotional weight of the reconciliation. Ron's growth feels less earned because the estrangement is so brief on screen. The ending in the hospital wing is present. Score in the 8–10 range — incomplete and rushed, with important steps skipped.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Ron's two primary relationships in this book are with Harry (best friendship defined by devotion, rivalry, estrangement, and reconciliation) and with Hermione (friendship shading into unresolved romantic feeling, expressed as protectiveness, jealousy, and occasional cruelty). Secondary relationships include his family (Fred and George as a foil; Percy as an irritant; Mrs. Weasley as a source of both comfort and embarrassment), Krum (as an object of worship that becomes a source of jealousy), and Sirius (a trusted adult whose advice Ron helps solicit and process).
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Harry relationship is preserved in its emotional dynamic though compressed. The Hermione relationship is present with its jealousy component clearly shown. The family relationships are present in reduced form (dress robes scene with Mrs. Weasley, Fred and George interactions). Krum-as-idol-then-rival is present.
key_relationships.difference: The Sirius relationship is entirely absent from the film (no cave meeting). This removes a relationship that reveals Ron as a perceptive, engaged participant in the larger threat narrative. Ron's relationship with his brothers (Fred and George's business scheme, the leprechaun gold revelation, the blackmail subplot) is stripped down, removing scenes that show Ron as a younger sibling who genuinely worries about his brothers but is also excluded from their confidence. The dynamic between Ron and Hermione, while present, lacks the specific texture of his accumulated behavior toward her — the weeks of cold-shouldering that make his Yule Ball jealousy more understandable, and the 'next time ask me before someone else does' line's full emotional impact (which IS preserved in the film, almost verbatim). The Harry relationship's emotional dynamic is correct but its daily texture — the library sessions, the mutual silent suffering, Ron coming to believe Harry more gradually — is lost.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The core dynamics of the Harry and Hermione relationships are preserved in emotional tone, though compressed. The Sirius relationship is entirely absent, removing a meaningful relational dimension. The family subplot is reduced. The relationships are mostly faithful with significant compression. Score in the 7–8 range.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Ron in Goblet of Fire is complex precisely because he is simultaneously Harry's most devoted friend and capable of sustained, petty cruelty toward him. He worships Krum but becomes consumed by jealousy of Krum. He defends Hermione's honor against Malfoy but says genuinely unkind things about her and other girls. He is morally perceptive (recognizing the Dark Mark's historical terror when Harry doesn't) and morally limited (initially dismissing house-elf rights, dismissing Hermione's S.P.E.W. work, being cruel about Padma at the Yule Ball). He is funny in ways that reveal intelligence (the Divination homework ruse, the Trelawney impressions) and funny in ways that reveal insensitivity ('something's about to burst out of Eloise Midgen but I don't think it's a swan'). He has class consciousness that produces real emotional pain rather than comic resentment. The scene where he lies about how much money matters to him, the leprechaun gold revelation, the secondhand dress robes — these together paint a portrait of a boy whose cheerfulness is partly a performance over genuine material anxiety. His intellectual contributions to the mystery plot (Crouch analysis in the cave, the Bagman/gold connection, theorizing about Death Eaters) show a mind that functions well when not paralyzed by insecurity.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film preserves Ron as funny, loyal, jealous, and insecure about money. The dress robes scene is well-executed and his self-deprecating humor ('murder me, Harry') is on point. His Yule Ball jealousy is present. His moral limitations regarding Hermione are shown at the ball.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The intellectual and investigative Ron is almost entirely absent. The weeks of library research, the cave scene analysis, the Bagman theorizing — these collectively established Ron as a smart, engaged participant in the mystery plot. The film's Ron is reactive rather than active. His class-based pain is glimpsed (dress robes) but the leprechaun gold scene — where he admits 'I hate being poor' with real vulnerability — is absent. His moral limitations around house elves (which reveal a specific worldview, not just laziness) are absent. His sustained petty behavior during the estrangement, which complicates his otherwise sympathetic portrayal, is compressed into a single scene. The Divination homework ruse with Harry — a scene that shows their friendship at its most warmly inventive — is absent. The layers that made Ron simultaneously sympathetic and flawed, smart and insecure, funny and occasionally unkind, are reduced to primarily sympathetic comic loyalty.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: Significant nuances are lost: the intellectual Ron, the class-anxious Ron, the morally limited Ron (house elves), the sustained-pettiness Ron. What remains is the warm-loyal-funny-jealous surface. The character is recognizable but substantially simplified compared to the books. Score in the 8–10 range.

Ron's active participation in research for the second task (weeks in the library, Summoning Charm practice, Impediment Curse sessions) — mostly absent from the film
Cave meeting with Sirius: Ron's questions, analyses, and engagement with the Crouch/Snape/Moody mystery are entirely absent from the film
Leprechaun gold scene ('I hate being poor') — a key articulation of Ron's class anxiety and emotional honesty — is cut
Ron's intellectual contributions: theorizing about Karkaroff, the Bagman/leprechaun gold connection, asking Sirius probing questions about Crouch
The Divination homework ruse (inventing doom-laden predictions with Harry) — a scene defining their restored friendship's warmth and shared humor
Ron's sustained mockery of Percy and his commentary on the cauldron-bottom report — part of his verbal wit and sibling dynamics
Ron's moral limitations regarding house elves (the S.P.E.W. arguments) — absent from the film, removing a revealing flaw
Ron's unkind remarks about Padma Patil and Eloise Midgen — absent, softening his portrayal

The Fred and George blackmail subplot investigation, in which Ron worries about his brothers and considers telling Percy — absent, removing a scene that shows Ron's protective instincts toward family alongside his own ethical navigation
Ron's weeks of cold-shouldering Harry during the Hogsmeade visit (Harry uses Invisibility Cloak, sees Ron at Three Broomsticks) — absent

Ron's claim to have 'warned' Harry about dragons through a convoluted chain (in the film played as comedy/retroactive credit) replaces the books' cleaner emotional arc of Ron simply admitting he was wrong
score_caps_applied: Cap 3 (score above 75 if core book functions/decisions/agency transferred to another character): Ron's investigative and analytical function in the cave scene and library research is effectively transferred to Hermione or simply absent; applied to keep score at or below 75

Cap 4 (score above 70 if films preserve only broad identity but remove most defining book characterization): Partially applicable — the film preserves more than just broad identity, so cap 4 is not the binding constraint, but the combination of agency loss and nuance loss together prevent a score above mid-70s
key_observations: The film's Ron Weasley is recognizable and emotionally present in the story's main beats — loyalty, jealousy, humor, insecurity — but is substantially reduced from his book counterpart. The most significant losses are in agency and intellectual function: book-Ron is an active co-investigator who theorizes, analyzes, and contributes to solving the mystery; film-Ron is primarily a reactive comic-loyal presence. The class anxiety that gives his character genuine emotional depth is glimpsed but not dramatized. His jealousy arc exists but is compressed so severely that it loses its earned weight. The warmth of his friendship with Harry — shown in the books through shared humor, shared research, and mutual ease — is reduced to a few brief interactions. What the film gets right is the emotional core: the estrangement hurts, the reconciliation matters, and his devotion to Harry is never in question. What it loses is the texture, the intelligence, and the moral complexity that made book-Ron a fully inhabited character rather than a loyal sidekick.
